blocks.q: Spot the bug: two users click seat 12 of show 7 at the same instant. Both calls run the code below. What can happen, and what is the fix?
example_code: SELECT status FROM show_seat WHERE show_id=7 AND seat_id=12;
UPDATE show_seat SET status='HELD' WHERE show_id=7 AND seat_id=12;
a_bullets: Both SELECTs can return `AVAILABLE` before either UPDATE runs, so both users get a hold: a check-then-update race.
The UPDATE has no condition on status, so the second one silently overwrites the first.
Fix: one conditional statement, `UPDATE ... SET status='HELD' WHERE show_id=7 AND seat_id=12 AND status='AVAILABLE'`.
Rows affected = 1 means you won the seat. Rows affected = 0 means you lost the race, so reject that user.
The unique (show_id, seat_id) on `booking_seat` stays as a last safety net, not as the main guard.

blocks.q: The gateway delivers the same success webhook twice at the same moment, and the handler runs the statement below on both. Predict the rows affected for each. What does the unique index on gateway_ref add?
a_bullets: Both UPDATEs target the same row, so the row lock serializes them: one runs first, the other waits.
The first matches `PENDING` and affects 1 row, so it marks the seats BOOKED and confirms the booking.
The second then sees `SUCCESS`, matches nothing and affects 0 rows. It returns 200 and does no work: a duplicate.
The conditional UPDATE is what dedupes the two deliveries. The row lock makes it safe under a race.
The unique index on `gateway_ref` only stops a second payment row being inserted for the same gateway_ref, for example from a buggy insert path. It does not decide between racing webhooks.

blocks.q: A user pays through UPI and the webhook arrives at minute 9. The hold expired at minute 8 and the sweeper has released the seats. What should the webhook handler do?
a_bullets: Money was taken, so the handler cannot just drop the event.
In one transaction, try to re-take the seats with a conditional UPDATE `WHERE status='AVAILABLE'`.
If every seat was still free, mark them BOOKED, set the booking CONFIRMED and emit `BookingConfirmed`.
If another user grabbed even one seat, the booking cannot complete. Auto-refund in the same handler.
Confirm from the webhook, never from the browser redirect: the user may close the tab after paying.

blocks.q: Redis restarts and every hold:{show}:{seat} TTL key disappears while 500 seats are HELD. What happens to those seats, and why does the design survive it?
a_bullets: The DB rows still say `HELD` with an `expires_at`, and the DB is the source of truth.
The sweeper runs every 10 s and releases rows where `expires_at < now()`, so the seats free up on time.
Worst case, the release lags by about one sweeper interval, and the target is under 15 s.
If release depended only on the Redis TTL, those 500 seats would stay HELD forever and nobody could buy them.
Redis is a fast release signal and a cache, not the record of who holds what.

blocks.q: During a blockbuster queue, a user in position 40,000 refreshes the page. Why does their place survive, and what would go wrong otherwise?
a_bullets: The ZSET `queue:{movie}` uses member = user_id and score = arrival timestamp.
Join is idempotent: adding an existing user_id keeps the original score, so the position does not change.
If join created a new entry with the current time, a refresh would send the user to the back.
Users would then spam refresh or open several tabs, which adds load right when Inventory is protected by the queue.
One slot per account (login plus CAPTCHA) stops bots from holding many places.
